questions.question_text: Which of the following terms refers to the ability of a test to produce stable scores when readministered at different times?
questions.explanation: Test-retest reliability is the extent to which a test yields the same score when readministered under the same conditions at a later time. Alternateform reliability is achieved when alternative forms of a test provide roughly equivalent scores for an individual, and split-half reliability is achieved when two separate subgroups of items on the test yield similar scores. Content validity is the extent to which a test’s content can be said to adequately sample the area of interest, and criterion-related validity is the extent to which a test score correlates with scores of other tests for the same area of activity in an individual.

questions.question_text: In order for a test to demonstrate construct validity, which of the following conditions must apply?

options.text: The test score correlates with other measurements of the same area of activity.
The test measures a theoretical construct of interest, and scores on the test reflect this construct.
The test yields comparable scores at two proximate points in time.
Two forms of the same test yield comparable scores.
Subgroups of items yield scores comparable to those of other subgroups of items.

correct_answer.text: The test measures a theoretical construct of interest, and scores on the test reflect this construct.

correct_answers.text: The test measures a theoretical construct of interest, and scores on the test reflect this construct.

questions.explanation: Construct validity can be achieved only by demonstrating that the test specifically measures a theoretical construct of interest and that scores on the test are unrelated to similar areas. Establishing a test’s validity requires demonstration that the test measures what it is intended to measure. Three major types of validity can be assessed: content validity, criterion-related validity, and construct validity. Content validity can be achieved only if the content of the test can be said to adequately sample the area of interest. Criterion-related validity refers to the test’s relationship to independent criteria of an individual’s ability in a particular area (i.e., concurrent validity) or to the ability of the test to make predictions about future behavior (i.e., predictive validity).

questions.question_text: Prior to interviewing a new patient, you decide to administer a brief symptom questionnaire. Which of the following self-report assessment tools takes the least amount of time to administer?
questions.explanation: The BSI takes only 8–10 minutes to complete. The SCL-90-R (Derogatis 1994) is a revision of a much-used self-report instrument designed to provide information about a broad range of complaints typical of individuals with psychological symptomatic distress. The BSI (Derogatis 1993) is a 53-item self-report form of the SCL-90-R that assesses the same nine symptom dimensions and three global indices. The psychometric properties of the BSI are comparable with those of the SCL-90-R, and the BSI has the advantage of increased ease of administration, taking only 8–10 minutes to complete. The MMPI-2 (Hathaway and McKinley 1989) is also an efficient self-report assessment tool but with 567 items would take longer to complete. The PAI (Morey 1991) has 344 items and focuses on personality disorders. The PANSS (Kay et al. 1987), which assesses symptoms of disordered thinking, is a semistructured interview, not a self-report instrument

questions.question_text: What is the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) most useful for?

options.text: Assessing affective disorders and personality symptoms and disorders.
Assessing thought disorders and personality symptoms and disorders.
Assessing personality symptoms and disorders only.
Assessing a variety of symptom patterns, including thought disorders, affective disorders, and personality symptoms.
Assessing a variety of symptom patterns but not personality disorders.

correct_answer.text: Assessing a variety of symptom patterns, including thought disorders, affective disorders, and personality symptoms.

correct_answers.text: Assessing a variety of symptom patterns, including thought disorders, affective disorders, and personality symptoms.

questions.explanation: The MMPI-2 (Hathaway and McKinley 1989) and its recent alternative, the MMPI-2 Restructured Form (Ben-Porath and Tellegen 2008/2011), are probably the most widely used assessment instruments in existence. There are several reasons for the MMPI’s extensive use, including its efficiency, its extensive normative base, the use of validity scales that indicate the patient’s test-taking attitude, and its impressive cross-cultural validation. Although labeled as a personality test, the MMPI was constructed to assess what are now categorized as symptom diagnoses and, to a lesser extent, a few dimensions of personality.

questions.question_text: The Beck Anxiety Inventory is a self-report questionnaire that is best used for which of the following?

options.text: Assessing whether a patient meets criteria for any mood disorder.
Assessing whether a patient meets criteria for panic disorder.
Differentiating between panic disorder and generalized anxiety disorder.
Distinguishing between somatic and nonsomatic symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder.

questions.explanation: The Beck Anxiety Inventory (Beck et al. 1988) is a 21-item selfreport questionnaire with a focus on somatic anxiety symptoms, such as heart pounding, nervousness, inability to relax, and dizziness or light-headedness. This measure takes approximately 5 minutes to complete and was designed specifically to discriminate between anxiety and depression

questions.question_text: A 27-year-old patient presents with a complaint of 'having a breakdown.' She denies alcohol use but mentions that she has experimented with Ecstasy in the past. Which of the following screening instruments would be most helpful in assessing the severity of this patient's substance abuse?

options.text: Alcohol Use Disorders and Associated Disabilities Interview Schedule, DSM-IV Version.
University of Rhode Island Change Assessment.

questions.explanation: Psychological distress and dysfunction arising from the abuse of a wide variety of substances is a frequent reason for seeking psychological or psychiatric treatment. General psychiatric semistructured diagnostic interviews provide substance-specific DSM diagnoses when administered by a trained professional. Other structured interviews focus exclusively on the misuse of substances. The Drug Abuse Screening Test (Skinner 1982) is a valid screening instrument for the abuse of drugs other than alcohol. The University of Rhode Island Change Assessment (McConnaughy et al. 1983) is a measure developed to assess a patient’s readiness to change in relation to the use of drugs, alcohol, and nicotine; it is not a screening instrument to assess for severity of substance abuse. The Alcohol Use Disorders and Associated Disabilities Interview Schedule, DSM-IV Version (Grant et al. 2001), is specific for alcohol use disorders and would not be useful in this case. The Eating Disorders Inventory—3 (Garner 2004) is specific for eating disorders, whereas the Anger, Irritability, and Assault Questionnaire (Coccaro et al. 1991) assesses for hostility and aggression.

questions.question_text: A 32-year-old man presents with a history of frequent angry and impulsive outbursts. Which of the following instruments would be the most appropriate choice for assessing this patient's ability to control his anger?
questions.explanation: The Anger, Irritability, and Assault Questionnaire (Coccaro et al. 1991) is a 42-question self-report questionnaire designed to assess several aspects of impulsive aggression putatively related to serotonergic function, and focuses primarily on the inability to control aggression. The Overt Aggression Scale—Modified (Coccaro et al. 1991) is a semistructured clinician interview that assesses aggression, irritability, and suicidality in the past week. The BussDurkee Hostility Inventory (Buss and Durkee 1957) is a self-report questionnaire that measures different aspects of hostility and aggression. The StateTrait Anger Expression Inventory—2 (Spielberger 1999) divides behavior into state anger (current feelings) and trait anger (disposition to angry feelings). Megargee et al. (1967) developed an overcontrolled hostility scale using Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory items.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most widely used self-report inventory of depression?

options.text: Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia.

questions.explanation: The Beck Depression Inventory—II (Beck et al. 1996) is probably the most widely used self-report inventory of depression. The inventory includes 21 items to assess mood, pessimism, crying spells, guilt, self-hate and accusations, irritability, social withdrawal, work inhibition, sleep and appetite disturbance, and loss of libido.

questions.question_text: A 22-year-old woman comes to you for treatment and reports a history of thinking about hurting herself. Which of the following is a general psychiatric assessment tool that also includes a specific measure for suicidal ideation?

options.text: University of Rhode Island Change Assessment.

questions.explanation: The revised Koss-Butcher critical item set on the MMPI-2 is a list of 22 items related specifically to depressed suicidal ideation (Butcher et al. 1989; Koss and Butcher 1973). The Beck Hopelessness Scale (Beck et al. 1974b) and the Suicide Intent Scale (Beck et al. 1974a) are self-report instruments specifically designed for assessment of known predictors of suicidal behavior. The University of Rhode Island Change Assessment (McConnaughy et al. 1983) is a measure developed to assess a patient’s readiness to change in relation to the use of drugs, alcohol, and nicotine. The PANSS (Kay et al. 1987) assesses symptoms of disordered thinking.

questions.question_text: A 72-year-old man is brought in by his family for evaluation because he has been having problems functioning at work and frequently misplaces objects around the house. After the patient receives neuroimaging, you also send him for neuropsychological testing. Which of the following testing strategies would yield the most useful information about this patient's cognitive functioning?

options.text: Focus on the results of the Wechsler Intelligence Scale to assess the patient's academic and occupational potential.
Use each neuropsychological test to assess function in only one circumscribed cognitive domain.
Before administering tests, estimate the patient's expected performance on the basis of his economic status, and then compare this estimate with the results on each test.
Order a range of cognitive tests and look for a pattern of good performance or common failures across tests.
Assess how much effort the patient exerts while completing each assessment.

correct_answer.text: Order a range of cognitive tests and look for a pattern of good performance or common failures across tests.

correct_answers.text: Order a range of cognitive tests and look for a pattern of good performance or common failures across tests.

questions.explanation: Assessing an individual’s performance on cognitive tests involves interpreting the pattern of performance and common failures on a range of cognitive tests.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man presents with memory problems after a recent stroke in the right hemisphere. What type of deficit would be most expected with a right hemispheric lesion?
questions.explanation: Visuospatial memory deficits are most commonly expected with right hemispheric lesions. Verbal memory deficits are associated with left hemispheric lesions. Learning and retention are mediated by the medial temporal lobe, especially by the hippocampus and diencephalon.

questions.question_text: In which of the following tests is the patient shown drawings of familiar objects and asked to identify the objects?
questions.explanation: The Boston Naming Test (Goodglass and Kaplan 2000) is a confrontational naming test sensitive to the presence of word finding difficulty. The Boston Diagnostic Aphasia Examination (Goodglass et al. 2000) includes sufficient numbers of subtests to provide a comprehensive examination of discrete verbal skills, whereas the Token Test focuses only on language comprehension, using multistep commands that increase in syntactic complexity (De Renzi and Faglioni 1978). The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale—4th Edition (Wechsler 2008) is a widely used intelligence test. The Complex Figure Test, sometimes called the Rey-Osterreith Complex Figure Test (Corwin and Bylsma 1993), assesses geometric constructional ability to gather information about visuospatial processing, planning, and organization.

questions.question_text: Which of the following instruments can be used to assess psychodynamic factors such as drives, unconscious wishes, conflicts, and defenses?
questions.explanation: Part of the “standard battery” used by clinical psychologists, the Thematic Apperception Test is a widely used projective process for assessing the patient’s self-concept in relation to others. Originally developed by Murray (1943), the test consists of a set of 30 pictures depicting one or more individuals. The patient is asked to make up a story based on each picture. The stories generated are then scored for the individual’s needs as reflected in the feelings and impulses attributed to the major character in each story and the interactions with the environment leading to a resolution. The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (Grant and Berg 1948) is used to measure cognitive flexibility and concept formation. The Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (Overall and Gorham 1962) assesses a broad range of psychiatric symptoms most relevant to inpatient populations. The Beck Depression Inventory—II (Beck et al. 1996) is a widely used self-report inventory of depression. The Anger, Irritability, and Assault Questionnaire (Coccaro et al. 1991) is a 42-item selfreport questionnaire designed to assess several aspects of impulsive aggression putatively related to serotonergic function. The instrument focuses primarily on the inability to control aggression

questions.question_text: The Global Assessment of Functioning Scale is useful for which of the following purposes?

options.text: Rating patients on a hypothetical continuum from psychological sickness to mental health.
Measuring the construct of quality of life.
Assessing the patient's degree of social adjustment.
Tracking the progress and impact of treatment.
Assessing activity limitations and participation restrictions.

correct_answer.text: Rating patients on a hypothetical continuum from psychological sickness to mental health.

correct_answers.text: Rating patients on a hypothetical continuum from psychological sickness to mental health.

questions.explanation: Several widely used scales of overall psychosocial functioning (i.e., symptoms, social and occupational functioning) that rate patients on a hypothetical continuum from psychological sickness to mental health are the Global Assessment Scale (Endicott et al. 1976), the Global Assessment of Functioning Scale (American Psychiatric Association 2000), and the Social and Occupational Functioning Assessment Scale (Goldman et al. 1992). All three rating scales are extremely easy to use, are appropriate for use in numerous contexts, and have been shown to be reliable.

questions.question_text: Which of the following instruments could provide information about the adequacy of the support system available to a 34-year-old schizophrenic man who lives alone?

options.text: World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 (WHODAS 2.0).

questions.explanation: The Social Support Questionnaire (Sarason et al. 1983) is an efficient method for assessing social satisfaction. This instrument provides information about available resources of support and the patient’s level of satisfaction with this support system. The WHODAS 2.0 (Ustün et al. 2010) is a 36-item self-report questionnaire used to assess the individual’s activity limitations and participation restrictions for the prior month. The ILS (Loeb 1996) is a self-report measure of an individual’s competency to perform daily activities and self-care. The BPRS (Overall and Gorham 1962) assesses a broad range of psychiatric symptoms most relevant to inpatient populations. The PANSS (Kay et al. 1987) is a commonly used measure of disordered thinking.

questions.question_text: How can routine and standardized psychological assessments that track the progress and impact of treatment be most helpful for the clinician?

options.text: By helping the clinician to provide more ethical and conscientious care for the patient.
By alerting the clinician when the patient is not improving as expected.
By improving the cost-efficiency and effectiveness of treatment in the setting of shorter clinical visits.
By documenting the patient's progress for legal purposes.
By demonstrating to the patient that the treatment is working.

correct_answer.text: By alerting the clinician when the patient is not improving as expected.

correct_answers.text: By alerting the clinician when the patient is not improving as expected.

questions.explanation: Once treatment has begun, routine, standardized psychological assessment can track the progress and impact of treatment among individuals and groups. Clinicians are typically optimistic about the patient’s treatment response and at times are inaccurate in their optimism and unaware of treat-ments that are not working. Many efficient, easy-to-administer omnibus measures have been developed that can quickly (via computerized databases) assess changes in patients’ symptoms, behaviors, quality of life, and functional levels during the treatment process. These instruments are designed to alert the clinician when the patient is not progressing as expected. With these data, informed decisions can be made about whether the current treatment is effective or whether another treatment should be considered. Possession of such indicators would enable the clinician to flexibly adapt treatment to patient progress and to communicate convincingly with reviewers about the current treatment’s effectiveness and the continued need for treatment.
